https://www.politico.eu/article/elon-mus.text: Tech billionaire Elon Musk applauded the German far right’s win in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, a result that sent shockwaves through the country’s political establishment and around Europe. “Well done!” Musk wrote on X in response to Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel’s acclamation of lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. Siegmund thanked the billionaire for his “support” and floated future cooperation, saying Germany could again become “a place worth investing in” if the party takes power in Saxony-Anhalt. Musk has championed the AfD for years, including during Germany’s 2025 federal election campaign. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has had a turbulent relationship with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and publicly attacked him this spring over Berlin’s criticism of U.S. policy toward Iran, posted a screenshot without commentary on Truth Social of Sunday night’s projected result. Advertisement Advertisement The AfD ultimately took 43.8 percent and 39 of 83 seats — three short of an outright majority — delivering its strongest-ever state election result and moving closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since World War II. The result had the party’s allies around Europe exulting. Italy’s right-wing Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini congratulated his “friend” Weidel and declared: “Another Europe is possible.” Austrian far-right leader Herbert Kickl said voters had torn down the political “firewall” around the AfD, while Spain’s Vox leader Santiago Abascal wrote on X that the result was “a great hope for Germany and Europe.” Hard-right Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe called the AfD “an inspiration.” Dutch far-right leader Geert Wilders also congratulated the party after the election results rolled in. Notably, Britain’s preeminent populist-nationalist leader Nigel Farage had not publicly commented on the result as of Monday morning, with France’s far-right leaders Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella also remaining tight-lipped. Mainstream shock While Musk and Europe’s right rejoiced, centrist and left-wing heavyweights around the continent sounded the alarm. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland could celebrate the result. French Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad called it “a grave moment in Europe,” warning that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be a solution.” Advertisement Advertisement Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed, called the AfD’s return a “catastrophic demonstration of the blindness of Europe’s centrist politicians” and said: “This disaster is their doing.” Giorgia Meloni’s coalition in Rome was split: Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, leader of the pro-European conservative Forza Italia, declared the result “extremely bad news,” putting him at odds with coalition partner Salvini. By Monday morning, Meloni, French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had not publicly weighed in — nor had EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-are-european-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MMvF In an age of geopolitical unrest, more and more countries want to have easy access to their gold reserves Image: CFOTO/picture alliance Advertisement Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security. To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane. The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis. The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness." France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated. The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of England Image: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland . The gold rush Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty . "The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said. In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs . A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade. Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said. "As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said. The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis. Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location. "Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said. Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast. He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market." "The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold." The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion). The US question While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making. Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries. That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors. Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets. As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around. US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leaders Image: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017 , it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States. Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves." (AP Photo/Beata Zawrzel) KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Mourners on Sunday laid candles and flowers alongside bullet holes in Krakow, Poland, after the city’s central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief. A 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire a day earlier, killing six people and wounding 15 before police shot and wounded him. Poland on Sunday began two days of national mourning following the attack the day before, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror.” The violence began Saturday at around 3 p.m. when the assailant drove through the Main Square, in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city. St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight, the first time the call had been missed since World War II. On Sunday afternoon, St. Anne’s Church in Krakow filled with mourners attending a memorial service. The square reopened soon after and locals and visitors alike showed up to reclaim it after the tragedy. “I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety,” Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. “In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.” Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds. Woman injured by shrapnel while saving another Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he’d felt as though he was in a movie scene. “It doesn’t feel real,” the British tourist said. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows.” Warsaw native Magdalena Frączak, meanwhile, was visiting Krakow with her friend when shots rang out and the gunman drew closer. “I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body,” Frączak told the AP. “I also saw him out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after he had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café.” On Sunday, she forced herself to return to the Main Square to grieve among other mourners. “I can’t put it into words. Because I knew that I would never come back to Krakow if I didn’t come in here,” she said. “When I found out that they had reopened the Main Market Square, I told my friend that I had to come here.” American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the “beautiful city” during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital. “I’m Polish, my parents were from here,” she said. “I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.” Police officers described as heroes Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.” Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead. A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground. The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon. “If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher,” Klęczar said. Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in. Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help,” Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.” Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24. The suspect’s dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts. “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy wrote in a statement on Sunday, confirming that Magdalena Oksińska was a third year student and that, additionally, the sister of an academy employee was shot twice. “Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a post on social media, accompanied by images of the artist’s colourful paintings. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.” The mass killing marks a grim first for Poland Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views. “Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference Saturday. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow. Both father and son had gun permits, they said. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising. The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target. The club added that the suspect “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.” Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects. Officials blamed the school attacks on online “glorification of violence,” and said that some of the attackers were active in the far-right environment. The Krakow shooter’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague. “We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland,” he said.
